paras.text: The COVID-19 pandemic, and subsequent lockdown regulations (2020–2022), disrupted the workplace and heightened employees’ uncertainty, anxiety and fear (Damghanian et al., 2023). Employees in the retail sector notably experienced escalated levels of anxiety and depression, with the industry being affected by store closures, economic uncertainty, customer challenges and employee health risks (Benchekroun et al., 2022; Choi and Marinescu, 2025). At the time, research focused predominantly on healthcare workers, first responders, medical students and the general population (Chen et al., 2021; Mayer et al., 2022; Seaborn et al., 2022) with Voorhees et al. (2020) aptly referring to retail workers as the forgotten frontline.

Rosemberg et al. (2021) portray retail workers as having been distinctly vulnerable and fragile during the COVID-19 pandemic. When most blue-collar workers started working from the safety of their homes, brick-and-mortar retail employees suddenly became the indispensable frontline workers having to contend with significant health and safety stressors for which they were untrained and had no prior experience (Ali Sulaiman et al., 2020; Blau et al., 2021; Elnahla and Neilson, 2021; Jacobson et al., 2022; Mayer et al., 2022). Direct customer contact heightened retail workers’ anxiety and stress because social distancing was difficult to maintain, and customer interactions were complicated by elevated levels of public anxiety. These aspects augmented the psychological demands and mental workload of retail employees, increasing their risk for anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress and burnout (Choi and Marinescu, 2025; Janson et al., 2021; Rodríguez-López et al., 2021; Swazan and Youn, 2023; Voorhees et al., 2020). Retail work consequently became a high-risk occupation at the time (Barbieri et al., 2022; St-Denis, 2020). Key phenomena observed in the retail environment were increased workload, existential fear and survival anxiety, job and economic insecurity, volatile and demanding customer interactions, feelings of disempowerment, lack of management support and recognition, and increased work–family conflict (Elahi et al., 2022; Elnahla and Neilson, 2021; Gaan and Shin, 2023; May et al., 2021; Rosemberg et al., 2021; Swazan and Youn, 2023; Voorhees et al., 2020). The psychological impact of COVID-19 on retail workers and limited research in this regard highlight the need for studies that inform the support and management of these workers during crises and catastrophic events (Damghanian et al., 2023; Gaan and Shin, 2023; Janson et al., 2021; May et al., 2021; Mayer et al., 2022; Voorhees et al., 2020). Knowledge about how to support and manage employees’ coping and resilience during periods of disruptive change is essential since subsequent mental distress can undermine motivation and heighten workplace attendance anxiety (Choi and Marinescu, 2025) and lead to poor organizational citizenship behaviors and a decline in employee integrity (Mayer et al., 2022; Swazan and Youn, 2023).

Organizations were ill-prepared to address the psychological effects of the pandemic on employee well-being, particularly in terms of supporting employees’ coping and resilience during this time (Azizi et al., 2021; Carnevale and Hatak, 2020; Hamouche, 2023). Retail organizations, in particular, encountered unique challenges in sustaining employee motivation, mental health and productivity (Ali Sulaiman et al., 2020). Studies noted the detrimental effects that unsupportive employers (Choi and Marinescu, 2025) and strained supervisor relationships (Gaan and Shin, 2023) had on the mental well-being of retail workers during the pandemic. However, explicit research focusing on the management of operations and employees during the COVID-19 crisis is sparse (Hamouche, 2023). Research focused mainly on managing remote or virtual workers (Bartsch et al., 2021; Lee, 2021) and healthcare workers (May et al., 2021; Mayer et al., 2022; Voorhees et al., 2020). The limited body of research that explored the experiences of retail workers during the pandemic focused on specific populations, such as part-time retail employees (Choi and Marinescu, 2025) and aimed to identify particular stressors in retail (Elnahla and Neilson, 2021) such as job insecurity (Ghani et al., 2022), customer conflict (Mayer et al., 2022; Northington et al., 2021) and perceived workplace safety (Mayer et al., 2022). Other investigations have sought to predict or describe the adverse effects of COVID-19 on burnout (Rodríguez-López et al., 2021) and general mental well-being (Janson et al., 2021; Mayer et al., 2022; Rosemberg et al., 2021).

Implications for organizational and management support practices are informed by insights derived from research identifying stressors as well as from conceptual reviews (Asongu and Rahman, 2022; Carnevale and Hatak, 2020) and secondary sources (Ali Sulaiman et al., 2020). There seems to be a gap in COVID-19 research focusing explicitly on examining and consolidating organizational support practices in the retail sector, and even more so from a salutogenic perspective. COVID-19 literature highlights the scarcity of and need for resilience research on retail employees (Asthana et al., 2024; Karanikas et al., 2023). As retail employees were thrust into high-risk frontline roles during COVID-19 without adequate preparation, increasing their psychological vulnerability, it is essential to examine practices that support coping and resilience to reduce distress, sustain productivity, and strengthen the retail sector’s preparedness and socio-economic stability in future crises. Moreover, examining management practices in this pertinent context may contribute to broader workplace resilience theory, particularly as the conceptual multiplicity of resilience complicates its operationalization (Smuda-Kocoń, 2024). Therefore, the aim of this study was to describe organizational and management practices that enable retail employees to cope and remain resilient under challenging circumstances within a unified framework that is theoretically grounded and pragmatically useful. To achieve this aim, the following research question directed the research: How do organizational and management practices in a retail organization support employee coping and resilience during disruptive change such as the COVID-19 pandemic, and what insights do these practices offer for managing employees in high-risk circumstances and for the advancement of resilience theory? The study entailed an exploratory and descriptive qualitative inquiry, conducted from a hermeneutic phenomenological perspective. Salutogenic theory was applied as interpretive lens guiding analysis to focus on what went right, rather than what went wrong (Louw and Mayer, 2014).

Salutogenesis, a positive psychology approach (Louw and Mayer, 2014) conceptualizes health and illness as opposite ends of a continuum, rather than separate states (Forooraghi et al., 2022). Coined by Antonovsky (1987) it emphasizes factors that promote health rather than those that cause illness. In response to calls for increased visibility of salutogenic approaches in work-related research and practice (Jenny et al., 2022; Mana et al., 2021; Sethuraman, 2020), the study’s theoretical framework was guided by salutogenic constructs, specifically resilience and sense of coherence (SOC).

Resilience, defined initially as an individual’s capacity to adjust to adversity (Burnard and Bhamra, 2019), has since evolved to encompass systems and process-based perspectives. The systems perspective acknowledges that resilience is impacted by both external and internal influences and operates across multiple systemic levels, including the individual, group and organizational domains (Galy et al., 2023). The process perspective recognizes resilience not only as a reactive coping resource but also as a dynamic developmental capacity through which individuals and organizations can strengthen and grow from adverse circumstances (Burnard and Bhamra, 2019; Hartmann et al., 2020; Van Breda, 2018). Adaptation and recovery are thus recognized as the two core components of resilience within an organizational system (Galy et al., 2023; Wut et al., 2022). Organizational and individual resilience are interdependent constructs shaping each other (Ben-Hador and Yitshaki, 2025). Organizational resilience is defined as the organization’s capacity to respond constructively to disruptive and threatening circumstances (Wut et al., 2022) and to transform itself to support sustained functionality and long-term adaptability (Southwick et al., 2014). Individual resilience is conceptualized as psychological resilience, an internal, personal resource that enables individuals to withstand, recover from, and grow through stressors (Den Hartigh and Hill, 2022; Wut et al., 2022).

Developing and supporting employee resilience is key to organizational resilience, yet the measurement and operationalization of resilience remain challenging due to different resilience perspectives emphasizing different aspects of the concept (Den Hartigh and Hill, 2022; King et al., 2016; Sisto et al., 2019; Smuda-Kocoń, 2024; Vella and Pai, 2019). To support empirical engagement with the concept, psychological resilience has been framed within Antonovsky’s salutogenic paradigm (Antonovsky, 1987, 1996), which emphasizes positive strength-based constructs. Among these, SOC is often highlighted as a key resource for constructive coping and adaptive development in the face of adversity (Hartmann et al., 2020; Van Breda, 2018).

Sense of coherence is conceptualized as a resilience resource and a wellness-promoting life orientation, enabling individuals to perceive life circumstances as comprehensible, manageable and meaningful (Feldt et al., 2011; Roskams and Haynes, 2020). Sense of coherence supports resilient behavior in the workplace because it positively affects an employee’s capacity to cope with regular, acute or chronic stressors, thereby sustaining well-being and productivity (Forooraghi et al., 2022; Mana et al., 2021). The SOC sub-component of comprehensibility supports constructive coping as people cognitively make sense of their circumstances, perceiving them as structured, coherent and explainable. Manageability is the behavioral SOC component and entails a sense of having the needed resources to deal with challenges. Meaningfulness, the motivational component, supports coping because it enables individuals to perceive life’s challenges as worthy of engagement and exerting effort (Antonovsky, 1987; Feldt et al., 2011). Sense of coherence moderates the effect of adverse conditions on employee well-being (Broetje et al., 2020; Jenny et al., 2022). In the context of COVID-19, studies have highlighted SOC as a key factor in reducing stress and maintaining optimal functioning at work (Barni et al., 2020; Mana et al., 2021). Sense of coherence, in turn, is influenced by job resources and coherent work experiences (Broetje et al., 2020; Jenny et al., 2022; Roskams and Haynes, 2020), underscoring the relevance of Work-SOC, experiencing the work environment as comprehensible, manageable and meaningful (Bauer and Jenny, 2007). Organizations, through its structures, strategies and culture significantly impact employees’ salutogenic health (Forooraghi et al., 2022). By providing structure, consistency and routine, organizations constitute a holding environment that strengthens employees’ SOC (Rob, 2013). The organization as holding environment relates to the system psychodynamic notion of containment, which describes the organization’s ability to hold employees’ anxiety in such a way that they can make sense of difficult circumstances, thereby increasing their resilience (Eloquin, 2016; Kahn, 2001; Petriglieri and Petriglieri, 2010). A holding environment is characterized by safe, reliable workspaces that allow emotional expression and enable rational thought and action (Kahn, 2001).

Research indicates a positive correlation between resilience and SOC (Kase et al., 2024). Broadly resilience refers to a person’s capacity to adapt positively to adversity and SOC, reflecting an individual’s orientation to life as being comprehensible, manageable and meaningful, enables the capacity to adapt positively under duress. However, due to various resilience perspectives (Smuda-Kocoń, 2024), proposing a conceptual alignment between resilience and SOC requires choosing a specific conceptual framework to resilience. The 3-Cs resilience framework of Reich (2006) was chosen here, because it proposes a conceptual approach to enhance resilience during times of crisis. It has not been empirically validated but theoretically outlines three psychological principles for organizations to cultivate: coherence, control and connectedness. The 3-Cs framework is useful for crisis management such as the COVID-19 pandemic as it provides a theoretical framework for developing interventions aiming to make sense of dire experiences and cope with debilitating emotions of fear (Barni et al., 2020). Reich’s (2006) framework also conceptually aligns with SOC, proposing that a supportive work environment should (i) address uncertainty and confusion (related to comprehensibility) by enabling coherence, (ii) offer manageable options to cope with the crisis (related to manageability) and thus regain a sense of control, and (iii) build formal and informal relationships that are emotionally supportive and motivating (related to meaningfulness) to establish connectedness (Barni et al., 2020; Reich, 2006; Sethuraman, 2020). Figure 1 illustrates the proposed link between coherence, control, and connectedness (resilience constructs in Reich’s (2006) 3-Cs framework) and the SOC sub-components: comprehensibility, manageability and meaningfulness.

The study is grounded in a hermeneutic phenomenological orientation and a qualitative research strategy. Hermeneutic phenomenology studies a phenomenon of interest by exploring people’s lived experiences and making meaning thereof through interpretive processes (Crowther and Thomson, 2020; Lindseth and Norberg, 2022). The approach was deemed appropriate to study people’s emotional and personal experience and how they made sense of the unique context of COVID-19. Furthermore, hermeneutic phenomenology allows for researcher interpretation and acknowledges the role of personal and theoretical predispositions. Consistent with a hermeneutic phenomenological stance, I recognize that I did not approach the study as a completely neutral or unbiased observer. While dealing with my own COVID-19 related emotions and work-life challenges, as a psychologist I was intrigued at the time with how other people were coping. In previous research I have demonstrated a preference for studying employee coping, sense of coherence and identity resilience in uniquely challenging work contexts. In this study knowledge is therefore constructed through a double hermeneutic process, which entails eliciting narratives of lived experiences that reveal participants’ understanding of their experiences and blends these with the researcher’s interpretations (Alsaigh and Coyne, 2021; Suddick et al., 2020). Semi-structured interviews were conducted, and thematic analysis, a popular hermeneutic-phenomenological strategy of analysis (Ho et al., 2017), was applied to construct meaning from the data.

Purposive sampling was employed, intentionally selecting participants who had experienced the research phenomenon and were willing to share their experiences (Alase, 2017; Ramsook, 2018). Participants were included based on their permanent employment with the company, active work during the first COVID-19 wave in 2020 and the second wave in 2021 and either having tested positive for the virus or having had close contact with someone who tested positive. Following the first wave of COVID-19 in 2020, 14 eligible employees were identified by the human resources manager (HRM), and a further 25 after the second wave in 2021. Willing participants’ contact details were provided to the researcher by the HRM, together with the role, store location and whether they had tested positive or had to isolate due to close personal contact. To limit further potential recruitment bias, the researcher privately contacted potential participants once lockdown levels were relaxed to Level 1 or 2, to arrange in-person interviews. Of the 39 identified employees, 12 were excluded because they were unreachable due to leave or work commitments. A few were also excluded because lockdown restrictions were increased again in mid-June 2021, which prevented in-person data collection. The final sample (n = 27) size considerations align with decision criteria such as the diversity of the staff population, the breadth and focus of the research question and pragmatic constraints (Braun and Clarke, 2021). The sample ultimately ensured good heterogeneity in the experiences shared, as it included frontline sales staff, support staff and managerial-level staff across various racial and gender groups at different stores. Data analysis furthermore provided adequately rich and varied thematic interpretations, allowing for thematic or interpretive saturation (Braun and Clarke, 2021). The 27 participants (11 after the first wave and 16 after the second wave), are detailed in Table 1. For confidentiality, participant codes are used: W1P1 refers to the interview with participant 1, conducted after the first COVID-19 wave, and W2P1 refers to participant 1 from interviews after the second COVID-19 wave.

Data were collected through semi-structured, in-person interviews, lasting approximately 60 min each. Interviews were conducted in a natural conversation style, initially establishing rapport, explaining the study and confirming principles of confidentiality and freedom to withdraw. Interview questions are depicted in Table 2 and focused on participants’ experiences of living and working during COVID-19 and how they coped during this time. Interviews were audio-recorded using a cell phone and transcribed by a professional transcriber. ATLAS.ti (ATLAS.ti Scientific Software Development GmbH, 2023) was used for data management and to support the organization of data analysis. All coding and themes were generated by the researcher and no AI-assisted coding features were used.

Thematic analysis (Braun et al., 2019; Braun and Clarke, 2012) was applied due to its suitability for large samples that are homogeneous in certain respects and heterogeneous in others (Spiers and Riley, 2019). The focus was on analysing data across data sets to reveal shared meanings rather than uncovering idiosyncratic or existential, ideographic meanings (Braun and Clarke, 2012; Spiers and Riley, 2019) while acknowledging the active interpretive role of the researcher in the interpretation process (Braun et al., 2019). As a flexible analytic method, thematic analysis accommodates both inductive (data-first) and deductive (theory-driven) reasoning (Braun et al., 2019; Braun and Clarke, 2012; Spiers and Riley, 2019), which was important in this study as codes and themes were initially directed mainly by data and the research aim. As the analytical process progressed, with iterative engagement across data sets, the researcher’s interpretive work became increasingly influenced by relevant resilience and SOC theory.

Thematic analysis entailed a recursive process of moving between and within six analytic phases (Braun et al., 2019). Firstly, to establish a deep connection and familiarity with the data, the researcher read and re-read the transcripts, while also listening to the audio recordings, and taking notes in the transcript margins in ATLAS.ti (ATLAS.ti Scientific Software Development GmbH, 2023). Secondly, the researcher identified interesting and relevant text sections in each transcription, rephrasing and condensing these sections of verbatim text into meaningful notes. Similar and recurring interpretations were further condensed, by constructing latent codes. A latent coding strategy refers to constructing deeper, implicit or conceptional meaning, from the condensed interpreted verbatim text (Braun et al., 2019). At this stage, data were transferred to MS Excel, creating tables with sections of text and corresponding interpretations. Thirdly, the researcher continued to categorize similar and overlapping codes into more comprehensive themes. The analytic trail from verbatim excerpt to condensed meaning to code, is depicted in the findings section for two sub-themes grouped under theme 2, in Tables 3, 4. During initial analytic phases 2 and 3, the codes and the initial themes were overwhelming and related to a wide variety of psychological constructs. To enhance clarity and focus, the researcher engaged with resilience literature, enabling a more focused alignment of codes to a refined set of resilience-related themes. The iterative work through phases 2 and 3 led to the fourth phase, namely organizing themes into a coherent thematic structure. In phase five, the researcher continued to move between data and theory to refine the conceptualization of each theme. The final phase entailed presenting the findings in a compelling and logical narrative related to the research aim.

Data quality strategies focused on ensuring credibility, dependability, transferability and confirmability of the findings (Loh, 2013). Findings were supported with rich verbatim to enhance credibility. A thorough description of the research design, the sample and how thematic analysis was operationalized provides transparency and rigor, which promotes the study’s dependability. The transferability of findings to other retail organizations was pursued by providing a detailed background on the context of the study, including the organization and the sample. Grounding the findings in relevant psychological theory further supported confirmability.

Taking a salutogenic perspective, this study explored organizational and management practices in support of retail employees’ coping and resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic. The findings articulate practices that enhance coherence, control, and connectedness by addressing uncertainty, helplessness and low mood, and thereby fostering resilience within the organization. The same practices invariably increase employees’ SOC, strengthening their comprehensibility, manageability and meaningfulness. Firstly, the company addressed uncertainty and confusion through practices that establish coherence in the work context, such as maintaining discourse about the company as protective of its people, retaining work consistency, and establishing clear COVID-19 response structures, protocols and procedures. A clear response structure corresponds with research recommendations emphasizing the implementation of relevant COVID-19 safety protocols, procedures and guidelines in the retail sector to curb employee distress (Choi and Marinescu, 2025; Mayer et al., 2022; Janson et al., 2021; May et al., 2021). The result was a workforce feeling safe, knowing what to expect and do at work and being clear about how to respond to pandemic-related threats and eventualities. Coherence practices thus enhanced comprehensibility, namely, employees’ ability to make sense of the pandemic and to think and react rationally in unknown circumstances.

Secondly, it was found that company practices helped restore a sense of control. This was achieved by sustaining a discourse of strength and success, providing methods and resources to address pandemic-related health concerns and demonstrating a strong leadership structure. Employees reaffirmed perceptions of the organization as strong and resourceful. The availability of healthcare resources and the establishment of socio-economic stability further enhanced their sense that the situation was manageable. These findings underscore the importance of the organization establishing and communicating job security as soon as possible (Ghani et al., 2022) and providing financial support to mitigate economic harm (Ashforth, 2020; May et al., 2021) during crises such as COVID-19. Effective leadership serves as a crucial psychological resource, strengthening employees’ confidence that reliable individuals are available to navigate current and future predicaments. The need for supportive leadership has been alluded to in COVID-19 studies highlighting the negative effect of poor relations with managers and supervisors, on employee well-being (Choi and Marinescu, 2025; Gaan and Shin, 2023). Practices aimed at alleviating helplessness were thus consolidated as those restoring control and supporting employees’ manageability, by strengthening their confidence in having the necessary resources to cope with pandemic-related stressors.

Thirdly, the company addressed employees’ feelings of isolation and diminished morale by implementing practices that responded to their fundamental need for connection. Practices nurturing connectedness included promoting a discourse that identifies the company as supportive and caring, establishing shared meaning and purpose in the workforce, and providing multi-level interpersonal support structures. These practices strengthened employees’ sense of belonging and purpose, encouraging emotional positivity and commitment to their work. Nurturing connectedness aligns with COVID-19 studies underscoring the value of social support (Ashforth, 2020), relationships and collectivism, for promoting employee well-being (Gaan and Shin, 2023; Ahmed and Akaak, 2024).

Integrating the findings with the theoretical framework presented in Figure 1 results in a salutogenic framework for managing disruptive change as depicted in Figure 3. The salutogenic framework vertically categorizes management and support practices into Reich’s (2006) 3-C framework, and aligns with how each practice category (coherence, control and connectedness) supports the three SOC sub-components. Horizontally the salotugenic practices follow three tiers which are further categorized into tangible and covert practices. On the bottom and middle tiers, the organization established tangible practices, namely (i) structuring (i.e., providing a COVID-19 response structure, a visible leadership structure and multi-level support structures), and (ii) methods and resources (i.e., providing work consistency, methods and resources to address health concerns, and a shared meaning and purpose). Covert practices are indicated in the top tier in Figure 3 and entail practicing sustained discourse about the organization being protective, strong and successful, and caring. Covert practices thus revolve around maintaining an organizational identity, with which employees strongly and positively identify.

Ultimately, the salutogenic framework proposes the organization as a holding environment, which is essential when employees experience disabling anxiety at work (Kahn, 2001). A holding environment reduces disturbing emotions and facilitates sense-making (Petriglieri and Petriglieri, 2010). The proposition constructed in this study suggests that an organization seems best positioned to foster resilience when it acts as a holding environment that engages SOC-supporting practices on both tangible and covert levels. Covert salutogenic practices support organizational identification (cf. Ashforth, 2020), a deep-seated, value-driven identity construction process related to the emotional reality of the organization (Armstrong, 2005) and to important stabilizing work identity dynamics (Brown, 2017). Organizational identification enables coping and commitment (Ashforth, 2020) and offers a collective defense against anxiety (Brown, 2017) or “organization-in-the-mind” that helps to manage vulnerability and anxiety in response to disruptive change (Armstrong, 2005). Tangible salutogenic practices must be implemented to reinforce organizational identity as such practices signal the real or lived nature of its underlying values (Ashforth, 2020). Tangible practices include consistent and clear work methods, as well as offering a range of accessible health and safety resources. Crisis response systems, robust leadership structure, and additional interpersonal support structures are needed to contain emotional disruption and guide constructive behavioral responses.

This study set out to address a gap in research about management and organizational practices that foster resilience during times marked by disruptive change. It was conducted during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, engaging retail employees who were particularly vulnerable to anxiety and stress at this time and are central to socio-economic stability and growth (Benchekroun et al., 2022). The study was guided by salutogenic theory as recent COVID-19 research highlights the critical role of enhancing employees’ resilience (Mayer et al., 2021; Ngoc Su et al., 2021) and SOC (Barni et al., 2020; Mana et al., 2021) in mitigating the pandemic’s adverse psychological impact on vulnerable frontline employees. In addressing the unique plight of retail workers as unexpected frontline employees, this study proposes a pragmatic salutogenic approach to how they can be managed for sustained resilience and productivity during a crisis.

The study contributes to salutogenic theory, explicitly aligning resilience in the organization with SOC, confirming the utility of the 3-Cs resilience framework during actual crises and suggesting salutogenic practices in a unified framework. Aligning resilience with SOC is useful because resilience remains broadly conceptualized with little agreement on its sub-components, resulting in inconsistent measurement (Kase et al., 2024; Smuda-Kocoń, 2024). On the other hand, SOC is a clearly defined, well operationalized and measurable construct (Moksnes, 2021) with stronger predictive validity for well-being outcomes compared to resilience (Kase et al., 2024; Keil et al., 2017). To strengthen resilience, research confirms that organizations should focus on work environments that enable employees’ SOC (Mayer et al., 2021). Existing studies however focus on job resources intended to enhance SOC, while paying comparatively less attention to organizational and management practices that contribute to SOC development (Broetje et al., 2020; Jenny et al., 2022). The salutogenic framework that was constructed through this study encompasses practices that support employees’ SOC on both covert and tangible levels, which organizations can follow to foster resilience.

The findings support the usefulness of the 3-C’s resilience framework conceptualized by Reich (2006), by offering examples of how these principles can be operationalized to foster organizational resilience during an actual crisis. Psychological resilience is typically regarded as an individual trait, characteristic or skill that can be optimized in the work context through training, employee assistance programs or counseling services (Asthana et al., 2024). This study rather offers a systems perspective to resilience in providing exemplary organizational and management practices fostering organizational resilience. In so doing, the study contributes to creating what Roskams and Haynes (2020) conceptually refers to as a salutogenic workplace design—synthesizing organizational and management practices that foster resilience into a pragmatic salutogenic framework.

The study presents some limitations. First, although the research was confined to one organization, data were collected from participants in various roles, branches and hierarchical levels, enabling rich understanding of the way the crisis was managed. Some differences in experience were apparent between non-managerial and managerial participants. Non-managerial participants predominantly expressed anxiety about their own health and that of loved ones, as well as job and financial concerns. They consequently looked to the organization for protection, continued employment, income and health related support. Managers, in contrast, expressed greater concern about containing virus transmission, safeguarding employees and customers, and ensuring the operational and financial survival of the business. No clear patterns distinguishing experiences between participants were further noted or deeper explored, which may be regarded as a second limitation. However, the study did not aim to conduct subgroup comparisons and participant heterogeneity was intended to enhance the richness and breadth of the data. Management accounts provided insight into organizational practices and strategies implemented during the time, while employee accounts illuminated how these practices were experienced, enabling a synthesis of these accounts into an integrated framework for guiding organizational and management practices during crises. Thirdly, the preconceived theoretical approach led to one way of conceiving the findings, which may differ when taking another theoretical stance. This is a relevant limitation, given that the conclusions were structured thematically using a specifically defined resilience and SOC framework. However, findings derived from hermeneutic phenomenological studies are not presented as conclusive and irrefutable facts, but rather as insights that enrich and expand the relevant knowledge base (Alsaigh and Coyne, 2021). Being guided by an appropriate theoretical perspective helped in constructing and verifying the conceptual insights and in organizing the findings into a meaningful thematic structure. The unique family-owned context of the study constitutes another potential limitation to transferability, as the participating organization was resource-rich and exceptionally supportive. Relying on the HRM as gatekeeper for participant referrals may also have introduced recruitment bias, potentially resulting in selecting participants with a favorable employer perspective. While these aspects may have contributed to the notable positive employee experiences, it also allowed for the identification of resilience-promoting practices that align with the study’s salutogenic focus. It is important to acknowledge that participants’ narratives reflected pervasive fear, uncertainty and survival anxiety. Negative experiences revolved around fearing the virus and loss of life (their own and of their loved ones); anger and uncertainty were directed toward government and law enforcement services; work-related challenges included transport difficulties and uncertainties about coming back to work after lock-down and isolation. The absence of negative organizational perceptions in the data may be attributed to the organization as a source of certainty and support during a time of illness, isolation and heightened fear. The organization provided certainty when they were uncertain; stability in a time when others around them lost their work and income, and meaning in having something to do and somewhere to belong. The uniqueness of the study primarily stems from its timing. Interviews were conducted when emotional experiences were fresh in the mind, yet participants had developed sufficient reflective capacity to articulate the organizational factors that supported their coping. In this way, the study capitalized on utilizing the COVID-19 pandemic as a poignant example for fostering resilience in organizations during adverse times.
